title: Request processing CPU surface mapping and lightweight mitigation notes
content:
Goal:
Map the CPU 'surface' of a single small-chat request (<= 128 tokens) end-to-end and identify low-effort mitigations that reduce tail and p50 latency without changing model code. Emphasis: operational safety — changes must be reversible and low-risk to multi-tenant clusters.

Context / motivation:
- Recent SLO alerts show rising p95 on light-weight routes. Heap of recent flamegraphs point to parse/tokenization spikes on small requests that dominate latency budget.
- Hypothesis: several small, additive costs (header JSON parse, proto decode, tokenizer boundary scan, GIL-induced scheduling jitter, allocator overhead when handing buffers between threads) create a 10-40% p95 pressure depending on traffic mix.

What "CPU surface mapping" means here:
1) Break request handling into discrete stages we can measure: net_recv -> header parse -> routing -> body parse/proto -> tokenizer pre-scan -> tokenizer encode -> request queue enqueue -> batch join -> model infer (out of scope) -> postprocess -> serialize/send.
2) For each stage, capture micro-latency and % of total CPU time across a representative sample (sampled pprof/py-spy + perf + userland timers).
3) Identify hotspots amenable to inexpensive mitigations (caching, micro-batching, pre-parse, allocator pooling).

Quick summary of findings (short):
- Header/json parse + small-body proto decode = ~18-28% of CPU of small requests. Regex-driven key extraction in our router is surprisingly heavy.
- Tokenizer pre-scan (utf-8 boundary + simple token heuristics) = ~22% on average, but highly variable with input language; worst-case +35% for long prefix whitespace/heavy unicode.
- Python-level scheduling jitter (GIL + many short-lived CPython frames) contributes ~6-10% extra latencies on p95 via context switches under high concurrency.
- malloc/free and buffer handoffs between parser thread and tokenizer thread show up as 6-9% in profiler (jemalloc arenas + cacheline churn); freeing in different threads is expensive on our kernel versions.

Experiments run (commands and notes):
- Workload: synthetic small-chat requests (prompt ~40-120 chars), 1000rps sustained, 16 concurrent worker threads, 4 replica nodes.
- Profiling stacks captured via: py-spy record --format flamegraph -o run1.svg --pid <srv_pid> while running load test. Also perf record -g -p <pid> -- sleep 60; perf script | flamegraph.pl > perf.svg for native ops.
- Microbench harness: bench/request-stage-timer (go harness) that emits stage timings to stdout and to an in-memory histogram for 5m windows.

Representative numbers (baseline):
- median end-to-end CPU-time (excluding model infer): 0.95 ms
- p95 end-to-end CPU-time: 3.6 ms
- Breakdown (p50 / p95 approximate):
  - net_recv & socket buffer: 0.05ms / 0.15ms
  - header JSON parse + routing: 0.22ms / 0.85ms
  - proto body decode: 0.15ms / 0.45ms
  - tokenizer pre-scan + boundary detection: 0.28ms / 1.2ms
  - tokenizer encode (byte->ids): 0.12ms / 0.5ms
  - request enqueue + queue contention: 0.05ms / 0.3ms
  - buffer alloc/free + small object churn: 0.08ms / 0.3ms
  - python scheduling overhead (GIL contention + tiny syscalls): 0.05ms / 0.6ms

Notes on variability:
- When inputs have long leading whitespace or many CJK characters, tokenizer pre-scan spikes; this matches py-spy samples which show utf8-simd and utf8-scan routines hot.
- Under bursty arrival (100ms spike), queue contention pushes up enqueue delays and increases context-switch-related costs; p95 increases by ~60%.

Low-cost mitigations attempted and results:
1) Header parse micro-cache (per-connection): cache the parsed routing predicate (small LRU 1024 entries keyed by header checksum).
   - Result: header parse time reduced by ~65% for cached requests. Overall p95 down from 3.6ms to 3.0ms on synthetic workloads with 30% repeated callers. Risk: stale routing if header semantics change; mitigated via short TTL and explicit invalidation on config push.

2) Opportunistic fast-path for tiny JSON bodies: very small hand-rolled parser that extracts known keys using byte-search (fast-path enabled via content-length < 256 and limited char-set).
   - Result: ~40% reduction in header+body parse cost for eligible requests. Complexity tradeoff: code duplication, careful testing required.

3) Tokenizer pre-scan sampling + early-accept: sample heavy unicode runs and apply a conservative fast-token-path that treats long sequences as raw tokens and defers expensive boundary heuristics until necessary.
   - Result: average tokenizer pre-scan CPU down 18% overall, p95 improvement only on worst-case inputs. Risk: potential small differences in token splitting which we flagged to product (minimal impact on model quality for short prompts).

4) Per-thread small object allocator (simple slab pool) for buffer reuse across parse->tokenizer handoff.
   - Implemented a tiny freelist per worker for 4KB buffers.
   - Result: allocator-related CPU down ~55% in synthetic tests, p95 end-to-end improved by ~6-8%. Observed fewer cross-thread frees and reduced churn in jemalloc arenas.

5) Cooperative yield points / reduce frame depth in hot-path Python code: refactor the incoming request acceptance to keep C-level loops and minimize Python-visible call depth, also reduce creation of short-lived generator objects.
   - Result: small but measurable reduction in scheduling jitter; p95 decreased ~4% on high-concurrency runs. Cleaner stack traces in py-spy.

Controlled regressions we observed:
- Fast-path JSON: removed some validation checks -> occasional silent header-parse misses in fuzz tests (caught during QA). Rolling out requires stricter validation at inbound guard.
- Tokenizer early-accept: produced slightly different token offsets for a few edge-case emojis; tracked via eval harness and flagged to eval team.

Actionable next steps (short-term, low-risk):
- Ship per-worker buffer freelist (rollback via feature flag). Owner: Miguel. ETA: 2 weeks for rollout + 1 week canary.
- Add header-parse LRU cache with 30s TTL behind feature flag; instrument misses and errors. Owner: Ravi. ETA: 1 week.
- Add a safety-mode in tokenizer early-accept: run fast-path but record checksum and occasionally double-validate a sample (1% qps) to ensure parity. Owner: Claire. ETA: 3 weeks.

Longer-term ideas (research):
- Explore moving JSON/routing parse into a tiny native extension (Rust) to reduce Python frame overhead; measure ops cost of ffi bridge.
- Consider unified fast-path in front of request pipeline that maintains a tiny bloom filter keyed by header hashes to bypass full parse for repeat call patterns.
- Investigate kernel upgrades and jemalloc tuning to reduce cross-thread free penalties observed; test per-core arenas settings and coalesced free hooks.

Instrumentation and observability changes required:
- Emit stage-level histograms to metrics (prometheus histograms): header_parse_ms, body_decode_ms, tokenizer_prescan_ms, buffer_alloc_ms, scheduling_block_ms. This will let SRE create SLO alerts closer to true causes.
- Add stack-sample alerting when p95 > 2x median for > 2m to auto-trigger py-spy capture.

Open questions / things to validate:
- How often do real customers hit the pathological unicode-heavy inputs? We need traffic sampling before enabling tokenizer fast-path prod-wide.
- Does the per-worker freelist increase memory pressure on low-load nodes (we saw slight resident memory increase on microbench). Need a mem-safety cap.
- Can we upstream the tiny JSON fast-path into shared libs to reduce duplication across services?

Appendix: quick commands / snippets used
- perf + flamegraph: sudo perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -g -- sleep 60; sudo perf script | ~/flamegraph/flamegraph.pl > perf.svg
- py-spy sampling: py-spy record --output pyspy.svg --format flamegraph -- python -m loadtest harness.py
- microbench: go run cmd/stagebench/main.go --workers=16 --rps=1000 --duration=5m --payload=small-chat.json

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic: pick the low-risk wins first (buffer caches, header LRU). If reviewers feel strongly about pushing native parsers early, call that out — I left that as a research path because it is higher-risk and will require cross-team API/ABI work.
- Please add any missing linked artifacts (bench harness PRs, alert IDs) to linked_artifacts.
